description:
Hi! I'm Ahmed, a marine navigation officer and grad student at ÉTS Montreal. Challenge: Flame in Freefall.

🔥 Our head start: my Master's project at ÉTS is on fire in microgravity, so we already understand the science and can focus on the AI solution.

I bring fire safety, risk analysis, Arctic field experience and team coordination.

Looking for: AI/ML, data analysis, Python coding, data visualization, design/video.

Let's help keep astronauts safe! 🚀
summary:
BlueSphere is an AI-powered fire safety copilot for the future Moon base. Lunar habitats will likely run at 30% oxygen or more at reduced pressure. This shortens spacewalk preparation but makes materials burn more easily. NASA's fire experiments in microgravity are public, but hard to find, compare and interpret.

BlueSphere turns 764 tests from 8 investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into one web app with five tools. The Atlas maps every test and shows where the data runs out. The Ranking scores the fire risk for the Space Station, a Moon base, a lunar rover and a ship to Mars. The AI assistant answers only from cited NASA sources and says "I don't know" when the data is missing. The Detection demo spots a fire from its gas signature: CO2 gives the alert, CO confirms. After the fire explains the dangers that remain once the flame is out.

Our key finding: in these PSI test tables, no solid material was tested above 22.2% oxygen, and no fire was tested in lunar gravity. BlueSphere makes this gap visible and becomes more cautious where data is missing, to help engineers choose a safe oxygen level for the Moon base.
details:
What it does

BlueSphere is a free web app that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA microgravity combustion experiments, with the Moon base as its main scenario. It has five tools:

  1. Atlas: every test on one map, oxygen level against airflow speed, by fuel type (solid, liquid, gas) and outcome. A coverage map counts the tests by oxygen level and gravity. An empty cell is a question that no PSI investigation answers yet.
  2. Ranking: choose an environment (Space Station, Moon base, pressurized lunar rover, ship to Mars, or custom), a material and a thickness. BlueSphere gives a risk score from 0 to 100, a confidence level, the oxygen partial pressure and the closest NASA tests. The weights are the team's expert choice (oxygen 30%, material 25%, ventilation 25%, thickness 10%, pressure 10%), and sliders let users change them.
  3. AI assistant: it answers only from a knowledge base built from NASA sources, cites every source, says "I don't know" when the information is missing, and refuses off-topic questions.
  4. Detection (demo): simulated cabin sensors whose timing follows NASA's Saffire-IV and Saffire-V results. The detector learns the normal level of the cabin, then watches how fast CO2, CO, oxygen and temperature change. CO2 gives the alert and CO confirms the fire. A final check says when it is safe to restart the ventilation.
  5. After the fire: what NASA saw once a flame goes out. In Saffire-IV, a flame that went out reignited when the fan came back; flamelets can keep burning below the extinction limit; on Mir, a flammable cloud remained after a candle went out. Every point cites its source.

How it works

We downloaded the test tables of 8 PSI investigations (Saffire-I, II and III, BASS-II, FLEX, FLEX-2, ACME BRE and CFI-G), cleaned them and merged them into one dataset. The method is in DATA.md on GitHub. The risk model combines five factors: oxygen (linear from 14% to 35%), ventilation (a bell curve that peaks near 10 cm/s, where NASA's guide says flames spread best), thickness, pressure and material. When an environment falls outside the tested data, the confidence drops and cautious mode adds a 10-point safety margin. Gravity changes the confidence, not the score.

Benefits and impact

  • Engineers and researchers see in seconds what NASA has tested, and what it has not.
  • The gaps become a clear list of the next experiments NASA needs, such as solid materials above 22% oxygen and fire in lunar gravity.
  • Teachers and students can explore real space-fire data and ask questions in plain English.
  • BlueSphere is a decision-support tool, not a safety certification.

Tools

Python, Streamlit (hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud), pandas, NumPy, Vega-Altair, the Anthropic Claude API (model claude-sonnet-5-5) for the assistant, and GitHub for the public code: https://github.com/Ahmediheb1/bluesphere. The demo video was made with SI tools: Claude for the animation and Kokoro, an open-source text-to-speech model, for the voice. It carries a visible "SI-generated video and voice" watermark.

What makes it creative

  • BlueSphere shows what NASA's data does not cover, not only what it covers. It knows what it doesn't know: where the data runs out, it becomes more cautious to protect the crew.
  • It follows the whole life of a fire: prevention (Atlas, Ranking), detection, and the danger after the flame goes out.
  • The name: in microgravity, a flame does not rise. It becomes a blue sphere.

Factors we considered

Crew safety first. Only NASA sources, each one cited. Honest uncertainty: confidence levels, cautious mode, and simulated data clearly labeled. Open data (PSI, CC0) and open code. A clear interface in English.
